Nice article.

If you use exim instead of postfix as your MTA you can have spamassassin reject spam in realtime instead of having it build up in a spam folder. This is much better in the way that false positives are handled, the sender gets an immediate bounce message so they know straight away the message did not reach you, rather than it being lost in a sea of junkmail inside your spam folder. Also, you get better control by using DNSBLs as spam scoring rules rather than as outright rejection criteria, you can use the DNSBLs that are more aggressive in their listing policies without getting too many issues from false positives.
The problem when you use aggressive listings, you may not receive some emails from Hotmail and som other servers.

Yes, if you use them for simple rejection. However, used in a scoring system like spamassassin and allocated the right score they are much better. The hard part is working out the right score, but that can be done by running the rule across ham and spam corpus or even by trial and error.

Also, as I said above, rejecting mail is less problematic than "losing" it into a spam folder, if it's rejected the sender knows about the rejection within minutes because he gets a rejection message in his inbox and can make alternative arrangements if the original email is urgent, whereas mail diverted to a spam folder is lost altogether in many cases and not noticed for months in other cases, out of sight = out of mind.
I've tried all scores. All I got is angry clients with lost emails. As a result sometimes emails got delivered after 30 hours

lost emails getting lost into a spam folder? That's the major problem with spam folders, we stopped using them at work because they're either a recipe for losing mail or a makework. If you check your spam folder every time you check your email then nothing is ever "lost" in there but it's just as much work as if everything went into the inbox with no spam filter at all. If you ignore the spam folder and tidy it out every few weeks then there's almost always something in there being overlooked. If you use message rejection instead of sorting then at least the sender knows straight away that the message wasn't delivered (unless of course the sender dumps all the rejections into his spam folder and only checks it every few weeks, but that's not really within the recipient's control).

If mail was sent it must have gone somewhere, and there are only 4 choices.

1/ It got delivered to a folder at the recipient's end, which folder would depend on the filters running at the recipient's server or mail client.

2/ it was rejected by a server en-route and a rejection message was sent back to the sender by the last server which accepted it.

3/ it was accepted then rejected by a server en route which then blindly and moronically trusted the From: address to send a fake rejection message to the purported sender (terrible form, we block these on sight at work including the "greylisting" variants)

4/ it was somehow discarded by a mailserver along the way.

The 3rd & 4th choices should not be happening, is very poor form for a mailserver, 4 I would go as far as to call that misconfigured and 3 is often an example of criminally irresponsible cost-shifting as bad as the spammers. If the mailserver is configured correctly that only leaves 2 options, accept or reject. You should be able to see which your server is doing by studying the logs.
